reconcile.connective: Harmonizers resolve the reversal by papponymy — Abiathar son of Ahimelech also had a son named Ahimelech, so both relationships can stand.

discrepancy.connective: Heinrich Ewald, with Movers and Thenius, judged the Masoretic genealogy simply corrupt — “Ahimelech the son of Abiathar” is an erroneous transposition of the original “Abiathar the son of Ahimelech.”

skeptic.name: Heinrich Ewald
skeptic.work: The History of Israel (Geschichte des Volkes Israel)
skeptic.attribution: Heinrich Ewald (d. 1875), The History of Israel (Geschichte des Volkes Israel, 1864)

excerpts.excerpt_text: But the expression “Ahimelech the son of Abiathar” is apparently a very strange one, as Abiathar was a son of Ahimelech according to Sa1 22:20 … We are therefore disposed to adopt the view held by Bertheau and Oehler, viz., that Abiathar the high priest, the son of Ahimelech, had also a son named Ahimelech, as it is by no means a rare occurrence for grandfather and grandson to have the same names
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: KD names the exact tension (Abiathar is son of Ahimelech in 1 Sam 22:20, yet 2 Sam 8:17 calls Ahimelech son of Abiathar) and offers the papponymy harmonization (a same-named grandson Ahimelech), which is the strongest reconcile on the row. The strange/grandfather-grandson clauses are joined; the intervening list of cross-references and the rejection of the transposition theory are elided without altering the sense.

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament (1861-75), on 2 Samuel 8:17
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: K&D treat this exact reversal at length on 2 Sam 8:17, weighing the transposition theory and defending the papponymy (same-named grandson) solution; surfaced harmonizing commentator keyed to the passage.
